confirmed.claim: The official ServiceNow API reference for RESTMessageV2 documents setStringParameter(String name, String value) as setting a named REST message function variable to a given value, returning void, with XML reserved characters in the value escaped.
confirmed.title: RESTMessageV2 - Scoped, Global
confirmed.reportedQuote: Sets a REST message function variable with the specified name from the REST message record to the specified value.

verdict.exactQuote: Sets a REST message function variable with the specified name from the REST message record to the specified value. XML reserved characters in the value are converted to the equivalent escaped characters.
verdict.correction: No substantive correction — every element of the claim checks out. Two caveats worth recording. (1) The reported quote is truncated without an ellipsis: it reproduces only the first sentence, which supports "sets a named REST message function variable to a given value" but NOT the escaping half of the claim. The escaping half comes from the immediately following second sentence ("XML reserved characters in the value are converted to the equivalent escaped characters."), so the claim is supported by the page but not by the quote as reported. (2) The "Returns" row is a table containing type "void" with an empty description cell — the page never writes the words "returns void" in prose. Confirmed details: signature is rendered as "RESTMessageV2 - setStringParameter(String name, String value)"; parameters are name (String, "Name of the REST message variable. This parameter must be defined in the REST message record before you can assign a value to it.") and value (String, "Value to assign the variable."); the page also documents the sibling setStringParameterNoEscape for setting a variable without escaping XML reserved characters. Page title matches as reported ("RESTMessageV2 - Scoped, Global"). Method-of-verification note: a raw curl of the URL returns only an 8 KB Fluid Topics JavaScript shell titled "Docs | ServiceNow" with zero occurrences of "setStringParameter", so the content is client-rendered and not visible to a plain HTTP fetch. I confirmed the wording three ways — two independent rendered fetches of the cited URL, the version-pinned Zurich copy of the same page, and a ServiceNow Community thread quoting the same two sentences from the official docs — which is why I treat it as genuinely present rather than reconstructed from model memory.

verdict.correction: No correction needed - the page supports every element of the claim. Two minor points of precision worth carrying into any write-up: (1) the page frames the four locations as named fields on the outbound HTTP method record ("Endpoint URL", "HTTP Header" and "HTTP Query Parameter Value" fields, and the "Content" field), not as generic parts of a request; (2) the page adds a caveat the claim omits - "When testing an HTTP method that includes variables, the Test value for each variable in the Variable Substitutions related list is used," i.e. the setStringParameter/setStringParameterNoEscape path applies when running the request, while the Test-value path applies when testing from the form. confirmed.question: The ServiceNow RESTMessageV2 API method setStringParameter(name, value): its official API reference page, exact signature, what it does (substitutes a ${variable} in the endpoint, headers or body of an outbound REST message at run time), and the difference from setStringParameterNoEscape (XML escaping).

confirmed.title: RESTMessageV2 - Scoped, Global (Zurich API Reference)

verdict.exactQuote: This method is equivalent to setStringParameter but does not escape XML reserved characters.

Use setStringParameterNoEscape to set a variable without escaping XML reserved characters." One pedantic caveat: the page never uses the words "the only difference." It asserts equivalence-except-escaping in one direction ("equivalent to setStringParameter but..."); the stronger "only documented difference" framing is an inference, though a sound one, since both methods are documented with the identical signature (String name, String value), identical parameter descriptions, and identical void return, leaving escaping as the sole documented distinction.

For example, you can change from a MEDIUM database type to a VARCHAR(100) database type if none of the existing data is greater than 100. [...] The system cancels any length change that results in data loss due to truncation.

[...] Note: You can change between string-based data types as long as length changes do not cause any data loss from truncation. For example, you can change from a MEDIUM database type to a VARCHAR(100) database type if none of the existing data is greater than 100. [...] The system cancels any length change that results in data loss due to truncation.

confirmed.question: ServiceNow string field maximum length: how max_length on a sys_dictionary entry works, the default of 40 for a new string field, the practical maximum for a string column, and CRITICALLY what happens when a value longer than max_length is saved - is it silently truncated or does it error? Also how to change max length of a field.
confirmed.claim: COMMUNITY SOURCE (not official documentation): the sys_dictionary max_length value is not enforced on save by the client or the server, so a value longer than max_length is accepted rather than rejected.
confirmed.title: Max length value of string field is not honoured - ServiceNow Community (developer forum)
confirmed.publisher: ServiceNow Community (community post, not official documentation)
confirmed.reportedQuote: Fields in ServiceNow accept string inputs greater than the sys_dictionary max_length value. [...] Despite the similarity of the name to HTML's maxlength attributes for input or textarea tags, this is not enforced as a limit in the client or server.

verdict.exactQuote: When you create a new sys_dictionary record to define a new string field, the max_length is mandatory. Despite the similarity of the name to HTML's maxlength attributes for input or textarea tags, this is not enforced as a limit in the client or server. Max length is not enforced on the Now Platform. Fields in ServiceNow accept string inputs greater than the sys_dictionary max_length value. This is the expected behavior of the product.
verdict.correction: Substance confirmed, with three qualifications. (1) Quote order: both reported sentences are verbatim, but the reported quote reverses them. On the page "Despite the similarity of the name to HTML's maxlength attributes..." comes FIRST, then the bold sub-heading "Max length is not enforced on the Now Platform", then "Fields in ServiceNow accept string inputs greater than the sys_dictionary max_length value." The "[...]" elision therefore implies an ordering the page does not have. (2) Provenance: the "COMMUNITY SOURCE (not official documentation)" label understates it. The text is not an independent community opinion — it is a near-verbatim copy of official ServiceNow KB0685779, "Why ServiceNow fields accept string inputs that exceed the max_length value" (published 2018-05-04, modified 2026-05-12), which the same reply links. The community post is the accepted solution by member "sandeepdutt" (Tera Patron), 07-02-2025, answering user Nisar3, whose max_length=30 field accepted a 43-character value. (3) Scope: "accepted rather than rejected" is not unlimited. The page immediately ties storage to the database column type (Small 40 = varchar(40), Medium 100 = varchar(100), Large 1000 / Extra Large 4000 = mediumtext), and the thread's remaining replies are entirely about where truncation then occurs. The official KB is explicit that the real limit is the column, not max_length: "The number of characters stored in a field is controlled by the database, not by the max_length value" and, under "Exceptions", "Some fields enforce the max_length value based on their database column definition. For example, the sc_task.short_description field is defined in the database as varchar(160) by default, which enforces a maximum of 160 characters." So the accurate statement is that max_length itself is not a validation limit, while the underlying column width still is — some fields do reject/limit input as a result.

confirmed.question: The ServiceNow sys_properties table: the maximum length of the Value field (believed 4000 characters), what field type it is, and official guidance on storing long comma separated lists in a system property. Also any documented guidance on using system properties for configuration lists.
confirmed.claim: The sys_properties table is the System Property table where properties are added, and every property value is stored as a string regardless of the Type selected — so a comma separated list is stored as ordinary string text.
confirmed.title: Add a system property — Zurich ServiceNow AI Platform Administration
confirmed.reportedQuote: All property values are stored as strings.

verdict.exactQuote: All property values are stored as strings. When retrieving properties via the gs.getProperty() method, treat the results as strings. For example, a true|false property returns 'true' or 'false' (strings), not the Boolean equivalent.
verdict.correction: Supported, but narrower than the claim's phrasing in two places. (1) The page does state "Some properties in the system aren't visible in an instance by default and must be added to the System Property [sys_properties] table" and, in the Value row of the form-field table, "All property values are stored as strings." The "regardless of the Type selected" wording is not on the page; it is a fair reading of the Type row ("Select the appropriate data type from the list (for example, integer, string, or true|false)") combined with the Value row's true|false-returns-'true'-string example, but the page never uses the words "regardless of the Type". (2) The page says nothing about comma separated lists as property values. That clause is an entailment of "All property values are stored as strings", not a statement on the page. The page's only mention of commas is the Choices field — "Comma-separated values for a choice list. If you need a different choice list label and value, use an equal sign (=) to separate the label from the value. For example, Blue=0000FF, Red=FF0000, Green=00FF00" — which defines the picklist offered on the property form, a different mechanism from a comma separated value stored in the Value field. Do not cite this page as documenting a comma separated (or name=value) property-value convention; cite it only for "sys_properties is the System Property table" and "all property values are stored as strings".

Three scoping notes, none of which defeat the claim: (1) this is release-note prose announcing a change of default, not a settings-reference topic — the page does not otherwise define or document what the host truncation limit does, so cite it as "the default was changed in 30.6.0," not as the canonical description of the setting; (2) the same sentence is a single combined bullet under a "Changed:" label that also raises the KnowledgeBase backfill limit from 100 to 300, so quoting only the 500-to-300 half is a partial quotation of one sentence; (3) the page carries no per-version permalink or anchor for the 30.6.0 entry, and 30.6.0 is not the newest release listed (30.6.3, August 2026, sits above it), so the version must be named explicitly when citing. confirmed.question: Qualys Policy Compliance API endpoint /api/2.0/fo/compliance/posture/info/ (Posture Information API): the full parameter list, in particular policy_id, policy_ids, details, truncation_limit. confirmed.claim: For /api/2.0/fo/compliance/posture/info/, the default truncation_limit is 5,000 posture info records per request (not 1,000), it is only valid when a single policy_id is specified, and the configurable range runs from 1 up to 1,000,000.
confirmed.title: Qualys API (VM and PA) User Guide, Version 10.40, September 7, 2026 — "Compliance Posture Information" chapter, Input Parameters table, page 1707 (truncation_limit entry); see also "Maximum Postures per API Request", page 1704
confirmed.reportedQuote: By default, a limit of 5,000 posture info records are returned per request (when “policy_id” is specified). You may specify a value less than the default (1-4999) or greater than the default (5001-1000000) to configure the number records returned per request.

verdict.exactQuote: truncation_limit={value}  (Optional) The parameter is valid only when the API request is for a single policy and the policy_id parameter is specified. By default, a limit of 5,000 posture info records are returned per request (when “policy_id” is specified). You may specify a value less than the default (1-4999) or greater than the default (5001-1000000) to configure the number records returned per request.
verdict.correction: No contradiction — the quote is verbatim (the only difference is that the PDF line-wraps "5001-1000000" as "(5001-" / "1000000)"), and both cited page numbers are correct: the truncation_limit entry is on page 1707 and "Maximum Postures per API Request" on page 1704, in the Version 10.40, September 7, 2026 edition as reported. Page 1704 independently confirms the default: "The output of the Compliance Posture Info API is paginated when your API request identifies a single policy to report on using the 'policy_id' input parameter. In this case, a maximum of 5,000 posture info records are returned per request by default." The single-policy restriction is reinforced in the policy_ids entry: "When this parameter is specified, all posture data is downloaded (and the 'truncation_limit' parameter is invalid)... When policy_ids is specified, truncation_limit is invalid." Two minor caveats, neither of which undercuts the claim: (1) the page never uses the phrase "not 1,000" — that contrast is the claim author's editorial framing, though the 5,000 default itself is plainly stated; (2) the claim's "range runs from 1 up to 1,000,000" omits that the page additionally accepts truncation_limit=0, which means no truncation limit at all (unpaginated, all records in a single output, with a warning about large XML). So the accepted values are 0 plus 1-4999 and 5001-1000000, not strictly 1-1,000,000. confirmed.question: HTTP URL length limits: what the standard says (RFC 9110 section 4.1 on URI length, and the recommendation that servers should support at least 8000 octets in a request line), plus real default limits in common servers: Apache LimitRequestLine default 8190, Microsoft IIS maxUrl/maxQueryString defaults, nginx large_client_header_buffers.

confirmed.title: RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics, Section 4.1 (URI References)
confirmed.reportedQuote: It is RECOMMENDED that all senders and recipients support, at a minimum, URIs with lengths of 8000 octets in protocol elements. Note that this implies some structures and on-wire representations (for example, the request line in HTTP/1.1) will necessarily be larger in some cases.

verdict.exactQuote: It is RECOMMENDED that all senders and recipients support, at a minimum, URIs with lengths of 8000 octets in protocol elements. Note that this implies some structures and on-wire representations (for example, the request line in HTTP/1.1) will necessarily be larger in some cases.
verdict.correction: The quote is verbatim and is genuinely the final paragraph of Section 4.1 (URI References), immediately preceding Section 4.2 (HTTP-Related URI Schemes); the #name-uri-references anchor resolves to that section. Two nuances worth noting. (1) Section 4.1 never affirmatively states that there is "no hard maximum" — it is silent on any maximum and only RECOMMENDs a minimum supported length. The explicit no-limit language lives elsewhere, in Section 2.3 (Length Requirements): "HTTP does not have specific length limitations for many of its protocol elements because the lengths that might be appropriate will vary widely, depending on the deployment context and purpose of the implementation." So "sets no hard maximum" is a correct inference about HTTP generally, but it is sourced to Section 2.3, not to Section 4.1. (2) 8000 octets is a recommended floor for supported URI length, not a cap or a target; Section 2.3 additionally imposes a MUST that a recipient parse element lengths at least as long as those it generates itself. The claim's characterization otherwise matches the page, including the request-line remark.

"When request filtering blocks an HTTP request because an HTTP request exceeds the request limits, IIS 7 will return an HTTP 404 error to the client and log one of the following HTTP statuses with a unique substatus that identifies the reason that the request was denied: `404.14` | URL Too Long ; `404.15` | Query String Too Long ; `413.1` | Content Length Too Large"

REACHABLE and the quote is REAL, but the page does not state the claim.

Verification method: raw curl returns only the Fluid Topics JS shell (8 KB, title "Docs | ServiceNow"), so I resolved the underlying content through the docs' own content API — map "Yokohama ServiceNow AI Platform Administration" (id VbEA8DxUy61CFZ25mbYrcQ), whose readerUrl is exactly /r/yokohama/platform-administration, topic "Available system properties" (id YagvDEsFnfX7Bb7LXpKzxw), 243 KB of real content. On the quote: it is verbatim and correctly transcribed. It occurs exactly once, as the description of the glide.attachment.extensions property (Type: string; Default value: none; Location: System Properties > Security). The reported quote is the first sentence of a two-sentence description; the second sentence is "No value means that there are no restrictions."

Why it does not support the claim: the page is a flat reference list of individual property descriptions, not a document about property design. "Comma-separated" appears 37 times, but every occurrence is descriptive of what one specific property happens to hold (roles that can create attachments, IP ranges, homepage refresh intervals, LDAP attributes, application names, etc.). The page contains zero occurrences of "standard", "best practice", "sanctioned", "pattern", or "convention". The only two hits for "recommended" are unrelated (a pointer to the Instance Security Hardening Settings doc, and the default ESLint rule set for glide.ui.syntax_editor.linter.eslint_config). There is no introductory or general guidance section on how to format property values — the intro only notes that some properties are reachable from the system properties form while others require direct access to the sys_properties table.

So the claim's two load-bearing assertions both fail. The page never "documents comma separated lists as the standard way to hold a configuration list in a single property value" — it never generalizes at all. And "establishes the pattern as vendor sanctioned" is an inference a reader draws from seeing many examples, not anything the page asserts. A citation of this URL can support only the much narrower statement that numerous out-of-box ServiceNow system properties happen to store comma-separated lists.

One incidental note for whoever relies on this page: its opening "Summary of Available system properties" block is explicitly labeled by ServiceNow as machine-generated ("This content was generated using new OpenAI-powered functionality. Results are provided on an as is basis and are not guaranteed to be accurate or complete"), so prose quoted from that block is not authored vendor documentation. The property descriptions themselves, including the cited sentence, are in the authored body below it.

No better URL: the given link is already the canonical reader URL for this topic, and it is release-pinned to Yokohama, which is more permanent than a floating "latest" alias. I did not find, and will not invent, a ServiceNow page that does make the general normative statement the claim needs; if that assertion is required, it needs a different source or should be dropped.

rejected.question: The ServiceNow sys_properties table: the maximum length of the Value field (believed 4000 characters), what field type it is, and official guidance on storing long comma separated lists in a system property. Also any documented guidance on using system properties for configuration lists.
rejected.claim: The character capacity of a string field such as sys_properties.value is governed by the Max length setting on its dictionary entry, which an administrator can change; ServiceNow documents the procedure but publishes no fixed maximum figure.
rejected.title: Modify string field length — Zurich ServiceNow AI Platform Administration
rejected.reportedQuote: You can modify the maximum character limit for a string field.

verdict.exactQuote: You can modify the maximum character limit for a string field.
verdict.correction:
The URL resolves (HTTP 200, redirecting to the canonical short form) and the reported quote is genuine and verbatim — but the page is much narrower than the claim.

What the page actually says, in full: title "Modify string field length"; intro "You can modify the maximum character limit for a string field."; "Role required: personalize_dictionary"; about this task "The URL type field hides the Max Length field on the Dictionary form by default. Browsers support URL length up to 2,083 characters. The URL field is a String field."; four steps (navigate to a form containing the field, right-click the field label and select Configure Dictionary, "Change the Max length field to the desired length.", "Click Update."); notes "You can change between string-based data types as long as length changes do not cause any data loss from truncation. For example, you can change from a MEDIUM database type to a VARCHAR(100) database type if none of the existing data is greater than 100." and "The system cancels any length change that results in data loss due to truncation."

Three mismatches:

1. "Publishes no fixed maximum figure" is not something the page states — it is an argument from silence. The page simply never discusses an upper bound, which is not the same as ServiceNow documenting that none exists. One page's silence cannot support a claim about what ServiceNow does or does not publish anywhere. The page does in fact print a character figure (2,083, for browser URL support) and names concrete database types (MEDIUM, VARCHAR(100)), so even the "no figure" framing is loose.

2. "Governed by" overstates the page. The page says Max length is where the maximum character limit is configured; it does not say the setting governs actual storage capacity, and it explicitly subordinates the change to the underlying database type — a length change that would truncate existing data is cancelled outright. ServiceNow's own support material goes further the other way (KB0685779, "Why ServiceNow fields accept string inputs that exceed the max_length value"): max_length is not enforced in client or server, and any string column above varchar(255) is created as mediumtext, so real capacity is not governed by the dictionary figure at all. Citing this page for "governs capacity" is therefore not just unsupported but arguably contradicted elsewhere in ServiceNow's documentation.

3. "Which an administrator can change" is narrower on the page: the stated role is personalize_dictionary, not admin.

The page does support the mechanical core — a string field's maximum character limit is set via the Max length field on its dictionary entry, and there is a documented procedure to change it. It does not mention sys_properties or sys_properties.value anywhere, so that example is the citer's extrapolation, not the page's.

What is the DEFAULT value of truncation_limit for this endpoint (believed 1000) and what is the maximum allowed value? How does pagination work (WARNING element with code 1980 and a URL for the next page)?
rejected.claim: WARNING code 1980 is the generic Qualys FO API pagination signal, but it is documented on the Host List API page (whose truncation_limit default IS 1,000) rather than on the posture/info endpoint — this Host List default is the likely source of the mistaken 1,000 figure.
rejected.title: Host List — Qualys Asset API online documentation
rejected.reportedQuote: 1980100 record limit exceeded. Use URL to get next batch of results.

verdict.exactQuote: Sample - Record Limit Exceeded Warning: "A truncated response is returned when the API request returns more host records than the truncation limit. In this case 1,000 host records are included in the XML output and the Warning message (shown below) indicates the URL you need to use to request the next 1,000 host records. ... 1980 100 record limit exceeded. Use URL to get next batch of results. ". Parameter table: "truncation_limit={value} Optional Integer Specify the maximum number of host records processed per request. When not specified, the truncation limit is set to 1000 host records. You may specify a value less than the default (1-999) or greater than the default (1001-1000000). If the requested list identifies more host records than the truncation limit, then the XML output includes the element and the URL for making another request for the next batch of host records."
verdict.correction: The page is real (HTTP 200, 300 KB of Host List documentation) and the reported quote is verbatim — 1980 with 100 record limit exceeded. Use URL to get next batch of results. appears four times (once per API version block, 2.0/3.0/4.0/5.0), and the page does state the Host List truncation_limit default is 1,000 ("When not specified, the truncation limit is set to 1000 host records"; also "By default, a maximum of 1,000 host records are returned per request"). But the claim as worded asserts three things the page does not say: 1. "Generic Qualys FO API pagination signal" — not stated. The page documents 1980 only for /api/N.0/fo/asset/host/?action=list. Nothing on it generalizes the code to other FO endpoints. (That generalization is true, but it must be sourced elsewhere: the VM/PC API user guide PDF contains 1980 13 times across different endpoints, e.g. the Authentication Record list sample: "19801000 record limit exceeded. Use URL to get next batch of records." with URL /api/2.0/fo/auth/?action=list.) 2. "Rather than on the posture/info endpoint" — the Host List page says nothing about compliance posture. Checked separately: https://docs.qualys.com/en/vm/qweb-all-api/mergedProjects/qapi-pc/posture/list_posture_info.htm contains no occurrence of "1980" at all, and its default is NOT 1,000 — it says "By default, a limit of 5,000 posture info records are returned per request (when 'policy_id' is specified)", and truncation_limit is only valid for a single-policy request (invalid when policy_ids is used). So the negative half is corroborated by that other page, not by the cited one. 3. "This Host List default is the likely source of the mistaken 1,000 figure" — pure inference by the citing author; the page makes no such causal statement and cannot. One further wrinkle the claim glosses over: the number inside the element is the request's own truncation_limit, not a constant. The sample says "100 record limit exceeded" because the sample URL carries truncation_limit=100 — while the surrounding prose on the same page says 1,000 records are returned and the URL gets "the next 1,000 host records", so the page's own sample and prose disagree. Anyone quoting this as evidence of a fixed 100- or 1,000-record pagination signal is over-reading it. Net: the cited page supports "code 1980 signals truncation/pagination on Host List" and "Host List truncation_limit defaults to 1,000". It does not support "generic FO API signal", the posture/info comparison, or the source-of-the-error speculation.
verdict.betterUrl: https://www.qualys.com/docs/qualys-api-vmpc-user-guide.pdf — the permanent Qualys API (VM, PC) User Guide PDF, which carries the same Host List sample and also shows code 1980 on other FO endpoints (supporting the "generic" half of the claim, which the cited HTML page does not). For the posture-endpoint half: https://docs.qualys.com/en/vm/qweb-all-api/mergedProjects/qapi-pc/posture/list_posture_info.htm (no 1980, default 5,000).
